chapter: Union career, Masons, mentoring and the Clef Club
title: Howard as a mentor to young musicians and the initiation fee break
summary: Collette says Howard inspired Hamilton, Mingus, Dolphy and others, and arranged a two-week reduced initiation fee for nonunion players.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well, Buddy said that you have helped a great many younger musicians in this town. He said he personally is very indebted to you. Maybe you can talk about some of the musicians that have come along that you've helped.

Well, one thing I can say, see we know so much about you, Paul, we just kind of want you to say what you remember and some of these things I'm about to say now are things that a bunch of the musicians in Los Angeles who have done quite well -- Chico Hamilton, Charlie Mingus, Jackie who is living in New York, Kelsoe, Britt Woodman, the whole Woodman family, the Woodman brothers.
Eric Dolphy. I could go on and on, a lot of young people, through the period of, say, '46, '42,

'48, around there, where some of the people were just beginning to play, some of us went to the Service and everything, but Paul was our inspiration, because he told us, you know, about studying, and he told us, you know, how to sort of behave. He told us also that it was more than just playing music. You told us, you know, as far as making time. You also helped a lot of us in the studios, I mean as far as doing picture work. At that time it was more sideline work than anything. But, you know, just telling us how we had to conduct ourselves, and being on time and all these things, which meant a lot to us when we were quite young and a little wild. But Paul knew that a lot of us could make it, and he had a lot of friends and people too that was telling us, that were telling us the same things that Paul had done. So you had set such a goal for a lot of the young musicians at that time. And also, if you remember this time, when we had a couple of bands that were non-union bands, and we were playing at the Elks on Central Avenue. We were playing all over town and really doing all right, getting writeups in the paper, and we knew that the union was a little upset at us, and there were a couple of people, and one in particular, which is Mr. Fain who was like a policeman when he'd come out, and we used to run and hide from him. (Laughter) But Paul had different methods. He called us in in a friendly way and said, 'I'd like to talk to you fellows. Maybe we can work out something.' And he did. He

called us in, and somehow he had gone to the Board of Directors and they figured a way to lower the initiation fee from -- you know the price maybe better than I do. It might have been $30.00 then. And they brought it down to maybe 12.00 or 12.50, for a period of two weeks, so that a lot of the young players who were playing non-union --

-- could get into the union. So naturally when he explained it to us, we took advantage of the two week period to get the reduction in initiation fee. But Paul, this is what I mean, we remember. This is why I told Pat, when I talked to her, I said, 'There is one guy that I would vote for, because I think he knows more about it, probably has done more than most of us will ever hope to do, and if we can get him to tell his story, I think that'll mean a lot to everyone. The story will finally be straight, how the beginning started and where the beginning inspiration came from,' and it came from you, not from anybody else I know. So we just want you to add whatever you can to that.
